turns.content:
• found a court judgment yesterday. Jordan owes $12,400 in defaulted debt. wage garnishment imminent. he never told me.

• i canceled the moving van. i called him a fraud to his face. now i have to co-sign a $3,400 lease by 5pm today or we lose the place.

• was that overreacting or just smart. tell me straight.

Both. You did a smart thing and an overreacting thing, and they're tangled together.

**The smart part:** Finding a hidden $12,400 default judgment with garnishment incoming — days before signing a joint lease — is exactly the kind of thing you *should* slam the brakes on. Co-signing or sharing a lease merges your finances with someone whose finances just proved to be a black box. Canceling the van bought you time, and time is the one thing you needed.

**The overreacting part:** "Fraud" is a conclusion, not a fact. Defaulted debts have a range of backstories — medical bills, an old co-sign gone bad, a judgment from an address he never got served at, or yes, straight-up irresponsibility he was too ashamed to disclose. Hiding it is a serious breach either way, but the difference between "reckless liar" and "panicked guy who buried his head" matters a lot for what you do next. You skipped the conversation and went straight to the verdict.

**About that 5pm deadline — don't let it stampede you.** A few hours is not enough time to understand a $12,400 judgment, and "sign now or lose the place" pressure is how people end up legally tied to someone else's mess. If you co-sign or take the lease jointly, his wage garnishment becomes *your* rent risk: his paycheck shrinks, and you're covering the gap or eating the eviction. Losing an apartment stings. Being on the hook for one you can't afford is worse.

What I'd do in your shoes today:

1. **Let the deadline pass, or ask the landlord for 48–72 hours.** Any landlord who'd rather lose a qualified tenant than wait two days is telling you something too.
2. **Ask to see the actual judgment.** Amount, creditor, date, whether he's made any payments or has a plan. His reaction to being asked will tell you as much as the document.
3. **The real question isn't the debt — it's the hiding.** Can he explain why you learned this from a court record instead of from him? Whether you stay together or not, *that's* the thing that has to get answered before you share a lease, a van, or anything else.

So: right instinct, hot execution. Protect yourself financially no matter what — but have the actual conversation before you decide he's a fraud.

• he told me it was his sister's medical bills. says he'll sleep in his car until it's sorted.

• i said no. he can't stay in our sublet tonight.

• was that too far. or was it the right call.

Notice what just happened: the deadline passed (or nearly), and suddenly there's an explanation *and* a dramatic self-punishing gesture. Both of those are worth slowing down on.

**On the "sister's medical bills" story:** Medical debt can absolutely end in a default judgment, and plenty of people take on debt for family. But this is now the *easiest claim in the world to verify*, because he can show you the judgment. Court records list the original creditor. Medical collections look different from credit cards, auto loans, and payday lenders. If it's really medical, one document proves it. If he balks, delays, gets emotional about being asked — that's your answer. Don't argue about the story; ask for the paper.

Also worth saying out loud: even if every word is true, he watched you plan a move, pack boxes, and book a van while sitting on a garnishment that would blow up your shared rent. The *story* might earn sympathy. The *silence* is still the problem.

**On the sublet:** You were not too far. Here's why — kicking him out tonight isn't punishment, it's refusing to let a crisis you didn't create get resolved at full speed on his terms. "I'll sleep in my car" sounds like accountability, but it also does something sneaky: it makes *you* the villain of a story where he's the one with the hidden judgment. You are allowed to say "not tonight, I need to think" without that making you cruel. His housing emergency is 24 hours old to you; it's been months old to him. He managed before you knew. He can manage one night while you get your head straight.

The one thing I'd watch: don't let tonight become a series of small softening steps — he sleeps on the couch, then stays "a few days," then co-signs the next lease because he's already there and it'd be heartless not to. If the relationship has a future, it survives you taking a week and demanding documentation. If it doesn't survive that, it wasn't going to survive the garnishment either.

So: right call on the sublet. Next move isn't forgiveness or exile — it's "show me the judgment, then we talk."

• 5pm is in three hours. i could lease a one-bedroom in my name alone. he could move in after he sorts the garnishment, no co-sign, no joint liability.

• but that puts me as gatekeeper to his housing. feels like a power move even when i mean it as protection.

• is that prudence or humiliation.

It's prudence — but only half-formed, and the half that's missing is the part that actually protects you.

Here's the thing your gut is catching: you've been framing this as "joint vs. solo," but the real exposure was never the lease paperwork. It's whether *your* housing stability depends on *his* undisclosed chaos. A solo lease fixes that cleanly. It also creates a new problem you just named yourself: you become his landlord, his creditor, and his judge, all while being his partner. That's a lot of roles for one relationship to hold.

So before you sign anything in three hours, get clear on what this arrangement actually is:

**The structural stuff (boring but important):**
- Most leases require you to disclose all occupants. If he moves in later without being added to the lease, you could be in violation of your own contract. Ask the landlord *now* what their policy is on adding an occupant mid-lease. Get the answer before you sign, not after.
- If he lives there and pays you informally, you may become his de facto landlord — which in a lot of states means if things go bad, you can't just lock him out, you'd have to formally evict him. That's a nightmare scenario nobody imagines in week one. Worth knowing it exists.
- Solo lease means solo rent. Can you carry $1,700 (or whatever half of $3,400 is, times two) alone for months if the garnishment drags? If yes, proceed. If the plan secretly requires his paycheck, the "protection" is decorative.

**The relational stuff (this is the part you actually asked about):**
Whether it reads as protection or humiliation depends almost entirely on how it's framed and whether there's a visible path back to equal footing. "You live in my apartment on my mercy until you prove yourself" is corrosive — he'd feel it, you'd feel it, and every argument would have a trapdoor under it. "Here are three concrete things — show me the judgment, set up a payment plan on the garnishment, three months of transparency — and when those happen, we add you to the lease" is different. That's not a gate, it's a bridge with a toll.

One caution though: don't let this become permanent limbo where he's a perpetual guest with no stake and no timeline. Resentment grows in exactly that soil. If you do this, write the conditions down, together, today — what "sorted" means, by when, and what happens if it doesn't happen.

And the honest floor under all of it: he has not yet shown you the judgment. You're designing housing policy around a story you've been told, not a document you've seen. Before the lease, before the gatekeeping question — the paper. Everything else is sequencing.

If he meets this reasonable, protective plan with outrage rather than relief, that tells you what the "sister's medical bills" probably were.

• so you're saying the solo lease is just window dressing unless i can carry the full rent alone.

• i can't. i make $68k. $3,400 is 60% of my take-home. i need his half.

• where does that leave me.

Okay, stop. Breathe. The $3,400 number was a distraction — you just said the quiet part out loud: **you cannot afford the life you were about to sign.**

The solo lease isn't a solution; it's just a different way to lose. You'd be betting your housing, your credit, and your emergency fund on a guy who just proved he hides financial landmines. Even if he's perfect from here, that garnishment hits his paycheck, and you're still short. The math doesn't care about his intentions.

Here's where that actually leaves you:

**Today, at 2pm:** You don't sign anything. You call the landlord and say, "I can't make this work by 5pm." If they have another qualified applicant, you lose the place — but you were going to lose it anyway when the garnishment hit and he couldn't pay. If they don't, they'll likely give you 48 hours because finding new tenants costs them money too.

**The real question isn't whether to sign — it's whether to stay.** And that's not a decision you make at 2pm with a moving van idling outside. You were ready to merge your life with someone who let you plan a future while sitting on a financial crisis. That's not a paperwork problem; that's a trust problem. Whether the relationship survives depends on what happens next — whether he shows you the judgment, whether he gets a payment plan, whether he demonstrates he can be transparent when it's hard.

But none of that is solvable in three hours, and none of it changes the fact that you need housing you can afford *alone* because right now, his income is unreliable.

**So what do you actually do?**

1. **Find a place you can afford solo.** At $68k, that means something closer to $1,800–$2,000 max. It might be a studio. It might mean roommates. It might mean staying where you are a little longer if that's an option. Boring beats broke.

2. **If you want to try to save this relationship,** he gets his own place while he fixes his credit. You date. You don't cohabitate. You see if he can be consistent over six months without your housing on the line. If that's too humiliating for him, he was looking for a bailout, not a partner.

3. **If the relationship is done,** you're just looking for an apartment you can afford. Which, again, is not this one.

The 5pm deadline was always false pressure — landlords use it because it works. But you were about to sign a document that would have made you legally responsible for $40,800 over the next year, half of which you don't have, relying on a man who just demonstrated he can hide $12,400 problems until they explode.

Losing the apartment is losing a bad deal. Losing your financial stability because you were afraid to lose the apartment is worse.

Can you stay where you are a few more weeks? Or is there a friend, a sublet, a month-to-month situation that buys you time to find something within your actual means?

• so i need a place i can afford alone. and he needs to stay gone until he fixes his mess. and that might mean we're just done.

• but three hours ago i was picking out curtains. how does it fall apart this fast.

It doesn't fall apart fast. It falls apart slow, and then you find out all at once.

Three hours ago you were picking out curtains because you were living in a story about the future — one where his paycheck showed up, where his past was clean, where the rent got paid. The judgment didn't create the problem. It just turned the lights on. The $12,400 was already there. The garnishment was already coming. He was already lying by omission every time you talked about square footage and commute times. The only thing that changed today is that *you know*.

That's the disorienting part — not that the relationship collapsed, but that the version of it you were planning around never actually existed. You're not grieving what you lost today. You're grieving what you thought you had yesterday.

And yeah, it might mean you're done. It also might not. You don't have to decide that today. Today you just have to not sign a lease you can't afford. That's it. The curtains, the future, the question of whether he can ever rebuild trust — those wait.

Let yourself be sad about the curtains. That was a real future you were picturing. It just wasn't the one that was actually available.
